::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
## TL;DR

Spreading crushed basalt on cropland draws down $\text{CO}_2$, but dissolving it also raises soil $\text{pH}$, and that moves the nitrogen cycle. Adding geochemical kinetics and $\text{pH}$-dependent microbial enzymes to the Community Land Model ($\text{CLM5}$) shows a $0.5–1.2$ unit $\text{pH}$ rise activates $\text{N}_2\text{O}$ reductase, cutting agricultural $\text{N}_2\text{O}$ by $16–35\%$ for a $12–20\%$ climate bonus on top of carbon capture, while pushing more ammonium toward volatile ammonia. After this module you can explain why $\text{pH}$ is the one knob both effects hang from.
:::

## How crushed rock removes carbon

Natural silicate weathering is the Earth's multi-million-year thermostat[^1]. Silicate minerals (like forsterite olivine or calcium/magnesium-rich basalt) react with dissolved carbonic acid in rainwater:

$$\text{Mg}_2\text{SiO}_4 + 4\text{CO}_2 + 4\text{H}_2\text{O} \to 2\text{Mg}^{2+} + 4\text{HCO}_3^- + \text{H}_4\text{SiO}_4$$

The resulting dissolved bicarbonate ($\text{HCO}_3^-$) and calcium/magnesium ions are carried by rivers to the oceans, where they precipitate into stable marine carbonate rocks for hundreds of thousands of years.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    AtmosphereCO2["Atmospheric CO2 + Rainwater (H2CO3)"] --> SoilAmendment["Crushed Basalt / Silicate Rock Applied to Cropland"]
    SoilAmendment --> Reaction["Rapid Dissolution & Weathering: Release of Ca2+, Mg2+, Base Cations"]
    Reaction --> DissolvedBicarbonate["Dissolved Bicarbonate (HCO3-) Runoff to Oceans"]
    DissolvedBicarbonate --> MarineStorage["Permanent Ocean Carbonate Storage (>100,000 yrs)"]
    
    Reaction --> SoilpH["Soil pH Neutralization (pH rises +0.5 to +1.5)"]
    SoilpH --> MicrobialShift["Shifts Nitrification & Denitrification Enzyme Kinetics"]
    MicrobialShift --> N2OSuppression["Suppresses N2O Emissions (Potent GHG Reduced)"]

    class AtmosphereCO2 indigo
    class SoilAmendment olive
    class MarineStorage plum
    class N2OSuppression sage
    classDef indigo fill:#1d4a62,stroke:#c97d62,stroke-width:1.5px,color:#ffffff
    classDef plum fill:#48304a,stroke:#c97d62,stroke-width:1.5px,color:#ffffff
    classDef olive fill:#5b6e34,stroke:#c97d62,stroke-width:1.5px,color:#ffffff
    classDef sage fill:#95a87f,stroke:#3b1a18,stroke-width:1.5px,color:#3b1a18
```

By pulverizing basalt to fine grains ($\lt 100\ \mu\text{m}$) and applying it to active agricultural fields, **Enhanced Rock Weathering (ERW)** accelerates this geological reaction from geological epochs into human-scale years[^2].

## What the pH shift does to nitrogen

Carbon removal has been modelled heavily; the soil nitrogen cycle it sits inside has not. When basalt dissolves, it releases base cations ($\text{Ca}^{2+}, \text{Mg}^{2+}, \text{K}^+$), consuming $\text{H}^+$ protons and neutralizing acidic agricultural soils:

Soil $\text{pH}$ is the single control knob that both branches of this pathway hang from: raising it accelerates nitrification and unlocks the final $\text{N}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{N}_2$ reduction step (the climate co-benefit, teal), while simultaneously pushing the ammonium-ammonia equilibrium toward volatile gas (the air-quality cost, magenta).

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
    Basalt["Crushed Basalt Weathering<br/>Soil pH rises +0.5 to +1.5"] --> NH4
    Fert["Applied Nitrogen Fertilizer"] --> NH4["Soil Ammonium Pool (NH4+)"]
    NH4 -->|"Higher pH shifts NH4+ / NH3 equilibrium"| NH3["Ammonia Gas (NH3)<br/>Volatilization risk rises: air-quality cost"]
    NH4 -->|"Autotrophic nitrification runs faster near neutral pH"| NOx["Nitrite / Nitrate (NO2- / NO3-)"]
    NOx -->|Denitrification| NO["Nitric Oxide (NO)"]
    NO --> N2O["Nitrous Oxide (N2O)<br/>GWP-100 = 273x CO2"]
    N2O -->|"N2O reductase fully active at pH 6.5 to 7.2"| N2["Inert Dinitrogen (N2)<br/>N2O emission falls: climate co-benefit"]

    class Basalt indigo
    class NH3 rust
    class N2 indigo
    classDef indigo fill:#1d4a62,stroke:#c97d62,stroke-width:1.5px,color:#ffffff
    classDef rust fill:#a04b2d,stroke:#c97d62,stroke-width:1.5px,color:#ffffff
```

### The two nitrogen feedbacks

1. **$\text{N}_2\text{O}$ Emission Suppression (Massive Climate Co-Benefit)**: $\text{N}_2\text{O}$ has a Global Warming Potential $273\times$ stronger than $\text{CO}_2$ over a 100-year horizon. At low acidic $\text{pH}$, the bacterial enzyme **$\text{N}_2\text{O}$ reductase** is structurally inhibited, causing incomplete denitrification that exhausts $\text{N}_2\text{O}$. When $\text{ERW}$ elevates soil $\text{pH}$ toward neutrality ($6.5–7.2$), $\text{N}_2\text{O}$ reductase is fully activated, converting $\text{N}_2\text{O}$ all the way to harmless $\text{N}_2$ gas[^3].
2. **$\text{NH}_3$ Volatilization Risk (Air Quality Trade-off)**: In the ammonium-ammonia equilibrium ($\text{NH}_4^+ \rightleftharpoons \text{NH}_3 + \text{H}^+$), higher $\text{pH}$ shifts the chemical balance toward un-ionized volatile ammonia gas ($\text{NH}_3$).

## Simulating it in CLM5

In our paper in *Geoscientific Model Development*[^4], we implemented explicit geochemical kinetics and $\text{pH}$-dependent microbial enzyme modules within **CLM5 / CESM2**. Global cropland results at $10\text{ t basalt ha}^{-1}\text{ yr}^{-1}$:

| Agricultural Region | Direct $\text{CO}_2$ Capture ($\text{t CO}_2\text{ ha}^{-1}\text{ yr}^{-1}$) | Soil $\text{pH}$ Shift ($\Delta\text{pH}$) | Soil $\text{N}_2\text{O}$ Emission Change | Net Climate Benefit Multiplier |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **US Corn Belt (Midwest)** | $2.1–3.4\text{ t}$ | $+0.72$ | **$-24.5\%$ reduction** | **$+16\%$ cooling bonus** |
| **North China Plain** | $1.8–2.9\text{ t}$ | $+0.48$ | **$-18.2\%$ reduction** | **$+12\%$ cooling bonus** |
| **Tropical Brazil (Oxisoils)** | $3.5–5.2\text{ t}$ | $+1.15$ | **$-34.8\%$ reduction** | **$+21\%$ cooling bonus** |
| **Western Europe** | $1.5–2.4\text{ t}$ | $+0.55$ | **$-21.0\%$ reduction** | **$+14\%$ cooling bonus** |

### Explore rate and starting acidity

Move the application rate and the baseline soil $\text{pH}$ to see how the $\text{N}_2\text{O}$ bonus and the $\text{NH}_3$ risk trade off:

::: {.sim-card}
#### ⛰️ Cropland ERW Carbon-Nitrogen Multiplier

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof rate = Inputs.range([0, 30], {value: 10, step: 2, label: "Basalt application rate (t/ha/yr)"})
viewof ph0 = Inputs.range([4.5, 7.5], {value: 5.4, step: 0.1, label: "Baseline soil pH"})

phClass = ph0 < 6.0 ? "Acidic" : (ph0 < 7.0 ? "Neutral" : "Alkaline")

deltaPh = Math.min(1.8, rate * 0.075 * (7.5 - ph0) / 2.0)
finalPh = ph0 + deltaPh

co2Cap = (rate * 0.24).toFixed(1)

// N2O reduction is highest when raising acidic pH toward 6.8-7.2
n2oRed = ph0 < 7.0 && rate > 0
  ? Math.min(45, (7.0 - ph0) * 18 * Math.min(1.0, rate / 15.0))
  : 0

// NH3 increase occurs as pH exceeds 6.8
nh3Inc = finalPh > 6.5 && rate > 0
  ? (finalPh - 6.5) * 12 * Math.min(1.0, rate / 12.0)
  : 0

bonus = (n2oRed * 0.65).toFixed(1)

note = rate === 0
  ? "Baseline cropland status: no active rock weathering carbon removal."
  : ph0 < 6.0
  ? "🌱 Highly Acidic Soil: Strongest N2O suppression response. Basalt neutralizes toxic soil acidity while providing a massive non-CO2 climate mitigation dividend."
  : "⚠️ Near-Neutral Soil: High carbon capture rate, but monitor surface ammonia emissions to prevent downwind air quality trade-offs."

card = (label, value, colour) => html`<div class="sim-readout">
  <div class="sim-readout-label">${label}</div>
  <div class="sim-readout-value" style="color:${colour}">${value}</div>
</div>`

html`<div class="sim-readouts">
  ${card("Baseline Soil pH", ph0.toFixed(1) + " (" + phClass + ")", "#cbd5e1")}
  ${card("CO₂ Captured", co2Cap + " t/ha/yr", "#10b981")}
  ${card("N₂O Slashed", rate === 0 ? "0%" : "-" + n2oRed.toFixed(1) + "%", "#38bdf8")}
  ${card("NH₃ Risk Factor", rate === 0 ? "0%" : "+" + nh3Inc.toFixed(1) + "%", "#f59e0b")}
  ${card("Net GHG Benefit Bonus", rate === 0 ? "0%" : "+" + bonus + "%", "#ec4899")}
</div>`

html`<div style="font-size: 0.9em; background: rgba(16, 185, 129, 0.1); border-left: 4px solid #10b981; padding: 10px; border-radius: 4px;">${note}</div>`
```
:::


### Data and code

- **Land Surface Model**: The modified $\text{CLM5}$ land surface biogeochemical model is hosted in the [CESM Development Portal](https://github.com/ESCOMP/CTSM).
- **Simulation Scripts**: Global spatial gridded datasets, soil parameterizations, and run scripts are archived on Zenodo[^5].

## Key takeaways

- Basalt dissolution turns $\text{CO}_2$ into bicarbonate that rivers carry to the ocean, where it is stored as carbonate for over $100{,}000$ years; grinding to $\lt 100\ \mu\text{m}$ makes the reaction run in years rather than epochs.
- The base cations released consume $\text{H}^+$ and raise soil $\text{pH}$ by about $0.5–1.2$ units, and $\text{pH}$ is the single control both nitrogen effects hang from.
- Near-neutral $\text{pH}$ ($6.5–7.2$) fully activates $\text{N}_2\text{O}$ reductase, so denitrification runs to $\text{N}_2$ and $\text{N}_2\text{O}$ (GWP-100 of $273$) falls $16–35\%$; the same shift pushes $\text{NH}_4^+$ toward volatile $\text{NH}_3$.
- Life-cycle assessments that count only inorganic carbon weathering understate the greenhouse-gas mitigation of ERW by $10–20\%$.
- Deploy first on acidic, heavily fertilised cropland (Brazilian Cerrado, Southeast Asian rice-paddy rotations, US Midwest maize) to get carbon capture, yield gains and nitrogen-oxide cuts together.
